About

This book is the notebook titled Naval. It holds 152 sources and about 278411 words. The list is All 152 Sources.

How to Get Rich names the show as the navall podcast, the host as Nivi, and the subject as the co-founder of AngelList. The caption spells the show "navall" and the company "angel lists." The surname is not in these sources, so this book uses the notebook's name, Naval.

Many of the shorter files are that same tweetstorm, How to Get Rich Without Getting Lucky, split into episodes. How to Get Rich is Nivi's collected cut of those episodes, about three and a half hours in his introduction. The same sentence can appear in a short file and in the long one. A quote on a concept page is tied to the file under it.

Three files are in the notebook and are not readable English. They are marked on the catalog. Their titles are not treated as things he said.

A paraphrase is marked. A block quote was checked against that source.

Naval

152 sources. About 278411 words. The notebook's name is Naval. The long episode calls him the co-founder of AngelList, on Nivi's podcast.

The argument, as these sources tell it

  1. Wealth is not money, and it is not status. Wealth is assets that earn while you sleep. Money is how wealth is transferred. Status is rank in a social hierarchy, and he says wealth is not zero-sum. → Wealth
  2. You cannot get that by renting hours. You need specific knowledge, the kind the tweetstorm keeps having to explain, and you need equity. If you can sell and build, he says you will be unstoppable. → Specific Knowledge
  3. Leverage multiplies judgment. He names three classes. Labor and capital are the old ones. Products and media that can be copied at no marginal cost are the new one. Accountability, under your own name, is how society hands you equity and leverage. → Leverage
  4. The returns are compound. Long-term games with long-term people are where compound interest shows up, in relationships, money, and learning. → Long-term Games
  5. Wanting has a price, and reading is a loop. Desire is a contract you make with yourself to be unhappy until you get the thing. Reading starts wherever you already are: read what you love until you love to read. → Desire and Reading

The notebook also holds long conversations, among them David Deutsch across several files, Vitalik on Ethereum, Matt Ridley on innovation, Kapil Gupta, and a Periscope from May 2020. Those are in the catalog. The concept pages stay with the wealth tweetstorm, because that is the spine the short files keep repeating.

What these pages do not do

  • They do not add a surname the sources do not use.
  • They do not repair the three broken captions, and they do not quote those titles as his lines.
  • They do not treat a line in How to Get Rich and the same line in a short episode as two discoveries.

Wealth

Wealth, money, and status are three different things in the tweetstorm.

Seek Wealth, Not Money or Status, and the collected How to Get Rich episode, walk the same distinction.

"wealth is assets that earn while you sleep"

Seek Wealth, Not Money or Status.

He keeps going: the factory, the robots, the program running at night and serving customers. The thing you want is the asset that works when you are not in the room.

"money is how we transfer wealth"

Seek Wealth, Not Money or Status.

Money, in that stretch, is social credit. It is the ability to have credits and debits on other people's time. Society owes you something if you created value. Money is the record of that, not the factory.

"status is just your ranking in the social hierarchy"

Seek Wealth, Not Money or Status.

"wealth is not a zero-sum game"

Seek Wealth, Not Money or Status.

His example is a house. Everybody can have one. Your house does not take away his. Status, a rank, does not work that way. The title of the episode is the instruction: seek the assets, not the rank and not the tokens.

The host of that episode says the tweets are the storm called how to get rich without getting lucky. How to Get Rich uses the same phrase.

"how to get rich without getting lucky"

How to Get Rich.

Specific Knowledge

The knowledge that pays is the part he says people keep misunderstanding.

"specific knowledge is probably the hardest thing to get across in this whole tweet storm"

Arm Yourself With Specific Knowledge.

Arm Yourself With Specific Knowledge says the set you need is specific knowledge, accountability, leverage, and judgment. He says he will throw judgment in even if that particular tweet left it out. Specific knowledge, in the same passage, is tied to getting paid, and he says the confusion is the idea that everything can be taught. The file goes on. This page keeps the warning: if it is a standard curriculum, it is probably not the thing he means.

Renting hours is the path he tells you to leave.

"you must own equity a piece of a business to gain your financial freedom"

You Won't Get Rich Renting Out Your Time.

You Won't Get Rich Renting Out Your Time says people think work itself creates wealth, and that this probably will not work. The piece you need is equity. The caption says "renting of your time." The title says "renting out."

The skill pair he names is sell and build.

"learn to sell learn to build if you can do both you will be unstoppable"

Learn to Sell, Learn to Build.

Learn to Sell, Learn to Build calls building the product the hard category, and says it is multivariate: design, development, manufacturing, and more. Selling is the other broad category. Both, he says, and you are unstoppable. One of them is not the claim.

Leverage

Judgment matters because leverage multiplies it, and leverage is no longer only other people and money.

"leverage is a force multiplier for your judgment"

Judgment Is the Decisive Skill.

Judgment Is the Decisive Skill says this is an age of nearly infinite leverage, and that the great fortunes are created through it. The first job, in that file, is to obtain leverage. Permission is one route he names there. The file continues into what permissionless leverage is.

The three classes are named in the short file.

"there are three broad classes of Leverage"

The Three Forms of Leverage.

Labor is other humans working for you. He calls it the oldest form, great in the old world, and a status game in the modern one: everyone is trying to become the lead monkey, so having people work for you is difficult. Capital is the second old form. The Power of Leverage quotes Archimedes on a lever long enough to move the Earth, and says humans are not built to understand leverage because our past maps inputs to outputs one to one.

The new form is a product you can copy without adding cost.

"products that have no marginal cost of replication"

Product and Media Are New Leverage.

Product and Media Are New Leverage dates that to the last few hundred years: the printing press, then broadcast, then the internet and code. You multiply effort without other humans and without raising money from someone else.

Accountability is how he says you get permission to use the older leverage, and a claim on the result.

"embrace accountability and take business risks under your own name"

Embrace Accountability to Get Leverage.

Embrace Accountability to Get Leverage says society will reward that with responsibility, equity, and leverage. The risk is under your name. That is the price of the equity in Specific Knowledge.

Long-term Games

Compound interest, in this telling, is not only a bank account.

"all the benefits in life come from compound interests"

Play Long-term Games With Long-term People.

Play Long-term Games With Long-term People says that is an insight into Silicon Valley and into high-trust societies. The compound interest he names is in relationships, in making money, and in learning. You start with what you have. A repeated gain on that pile is the force. The short file's point is to pick the industry, and the people, where that repeat is possible.

He says "long term" in the sentence and "long-term" in the title. Both are the caption.

Desire and Reading

Two practices sit beside the money tweets. One is about wanting. One is about what you read.

"desire is a contract you make with yourself to be unhappy until you get what you want"

Desire Is a Contract You Make to Be Unhappy.

Desire Is a Contract You Make to Be Unhappy says you become disturbed because you want something, you work to get it and you are miserable in the meantime, and when you get it you revert. The contract is with yourself. The unhappiness is the term of the contract, not a side effect he forgot.

A file titled Happiness Is a Skill You Can Develop is in the notebook. Its caption is not readable enough to quote. The title is the title. This page does not pretend the body states the skill.

Reading, in the file that is readable, is a loop.

"read what you love until you love to read"

Read What You Love Until You Love to Read.

Read What You Love Until You Love to Read says everyone he knows who reads a lot loves to read, because they read books they loved. He calls it a catch-22 and tells you to start where you are. A separate short file, Read the Best 100 Books Over and Over Again, is 89 words. The catalog has it. The sentence above is the one checked here.

Glossary

Labels as these sources use them. Caption spelling is kept when the quote is the source.

  • Wealth. Assets that earn while you sleep. Not zero-sum, in his house example.
  • Money. How wealth is transferred. Social credits and debits on other people's time.
  • Status. Your ranking in the social hierarchy.
  • Specific knowledge. The part of the tweetstorm he says is hardest to get across. Not the idea that everything can be taught.
  • Equity. A piece of a business. What he says you need instead of renting out your time.
  • Sell and build. The two broad categories. Both, and he says you will be unstoppable.
  • Leverage. A force multiplier for judgment. Three classes: labor, capital, and products or media.
  • Labor. Other people working for you. Old leverage, and a status game in his telling.
  • Product leverage. Products with no marginal cost of replication. Printing press, broadcast, code.
  • Accountability. Business risks under your own name. Society, he says, answers with responsibility, equity, and leverage.
  • Compound interest. The benefit of long-term games with long-term people, in relationships, money, and learning.
  • Desire. A contract with yourself to be unhappy until you get what you want.
  • navall. The caption's spelling of the podcast. Nivi is the host. The subject is called the co-founder of angel lists.

another good concept is consumer surplus and producer surplus which is the excess value that somebody gets even though they were willing to pay more the product was priced the same for everybody I get a lot of joy out of my morning coffee obviously I've made some money if my coffee cost twenty dollars I would pay twenty large my morning coffee but Starbucks doesn't know that it can't price the coffee twenty dollars just for me because selling the exact same product so I'm getting a lot of consumer surplus out of the coffee and all businesses generate consumer surplus it's a good thing to keep in mind when someone's harping about how evil companies are Amazon might be a trillion dollar company but I will bet you they're generating trillions of dollars in consumer surplus through convenience and willingness to pay there are a lot of people who are willing to pay more than what Amazon charges them for all their services

let's talk about NPV NPV is just the net present value of something it's when you say that stream of payments I'm gonna get in the future what is that worth today so a common example of this is you're joining a startup company and you're getting stock options and the founder says well this company is going to be worth a billion dollars and I'm giving you Oh point one percent of the company therefore you're getting a million dollars worth of stock what he's or she's arguing is what's gonna be worth in the future you have to discount that back to today you have to figure out what is that worth today and you have to apply a discount rate or an interest rate that takes into account the massive risk the startups face what you end up with is the price that it's worth today and that's the price at which a venture capitalist would invest in the company today so if that founder just raised around at ten million dollars and that company's only worth one percent of what the founders arguing your million-dollar package is actually worth ten thousand dollars so NPV calculations at a very rough level you should be very comfortable doing in your head
